title: Linear search and binary search
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its constraints.
Trace the example and reason about its data flow.
Identify complexity, boundary or safety considerations.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: Linear search examines elements until it finds a target or reaches the end. Binary search repeatedly halves the remaining search interval and requires the input to be sorted according to the same ordering used for comparison.
understand.whyItMatters: Choosing the correct search algorithm depends on data ordering, update frequency and input size. Binary search is not valid on arbitrary unsorted data.
understand.analogy: Treat an algorithm or data structure as a set of operations that must preserve a clearly stated contract.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace formal complexity analysis, C object rules or algorithm preconditions.

explain.narrative:
Linear search examines elements until it finds a target or reaches the end. Binary search repeatedly halves the remaining search interval and requires the input to be sorted according to the same ordering used for comparison.

Before implementation, state input constraints, empty-case behaviour, ownership and invariants. Compile with warnings and test representative, boundary and failure cases.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The interval is half-open [low, high). mid is calculated without adding low and high directly. The function returns an index or -1; the conversion to int requires the index to fit int, which a production interface should address.

practise.guidedTask: Trace low, high and mid for a sorted sample.
practise.independentTask: Implement both searches and test empty, one-element, first, last and absent targets. Document sortedness for binary search.
hints: The input to binary search must be sorted.
Use low + (high - low) / 2 to avoid a possible addition overflow.
Choose a return type capable of representing every valid index and the not-found state.
